prompt: Write a short blog post about a visit from friends. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the post only.
final_message:
# A Weekend Full of Familiar Faces

There's a particular kind of quiet that settles over a house after guests leave. It isn't loneliness, exactly. It's more like the hum of a refrigerator you only notice when it stops. That's where I am tonight, sitting among a few stray coffee mugs and one forgotten phone charger, grinning like an idiot.

Our friends Maya and Dev drove in on Friday evening, after six hours on the road and one very questionable gas station sandwich. They arrived tired and rumpled, and within ten minutes we were all sitting on the kitchen floor, because apparently that's where conversation lives. Nobody wanted the couch. We just wanted to be close to the snacks and each other.

We hadn't seen them in almost two years. That's the strange thing about long-distance friendship: you text constantly, you send memes at midnight, you know about each other's lives in highlights. But being in the same room is different. Dev still laughs with his whole body, folding forward like someone punched him gently. Maya still finishes my sentences, only now she gets them slightly wrong, which is somehow funnier.

Saturday, we showed them our little corner of the world. We hiked the ridge trail behind town, where the maples had just started turning, patches of orange and red against the grey. Dev insisted on stopping every fifty feet to take photos of leaves. Maya pretended to be annoyed, then took twice as many. At the top, we shared a thermos of terrible instant cider and agreed it was the best thing we'd ever tasted. Altitude and good company will do that.

That night we cooked together, which is to say I chopped onions while everyone else offered opinions. We played a board game that nobody fully understood, invented rules as we went, and argued about them with the passion of a Supreme Court hearing. Maya won, and has already announced she'll be bringing the trophy next time. There is no trophy. She will make one.

Sunday morning was slow. Pancakes, too much coffee, and the particular reluctance of people who know a goodbye is coming. We stood in the driveway longer than necessary. There were hugs, promises to visit them in spring, and Dev yelling something out the car window that I couldn't hear and will pretend was profound.

Now the house is quiet again. But it's a different quiet, the kind that's still warm around the edges.

Call your people. Better yet, drive six hours to see them.
